content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a new simulator, focused on embodied AI in interior home environments. They use the Unreal simulation engine, and construct 300 scenes and manually create 17k objects. They run sim2real PointNav experiments and a semantic segmentation experiment in the simulator.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths:
* The paper is well-written and the claims are easy to follow.
* I appreciate the amount of engineering effort that went into the creation of this simulation platform, creating all the objects, constructing all the scenes, and setting up the lighting. It is impressive!
* Unreal Engine provides many benefits as a highly powerful simulation platform that continues to grow and extend in its capabilities. It is great to see it being used for Embodied AI research.
* The authors plan to distribute all the assets, including scenes and objects, under a license usable for research.

### Weaknesses:

In general, I find the experiments very underwhelming.

**W1. None of the experiments use the high-quality rendering mode advertised throughout the paper, making it sound like it isn't necessary.** Instead, they only use the real-time rendering mode for all the experiments, and for the embodied PointNav experiment, they only train at 160x90 which loses all the photorealistic details in the images.

**W2. Why are there no interactive experiments?** There is a claim:

> 17,234 unique objects that can be manipulated individually

The paper advertises that their simulator is interactive, and only compare it to existing interactive simulators, but the experiments merely show it used for navigation and segmentation experiments. There would be much more value added if the authors could show it working well for interactive, manipulation-based tasks.

**W3.** Sim2Real PointNav has been done many times before ([1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.06321), [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.05873), [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.10821)). Sim2Real PointNav isn’t a new capability unlocked by InteriorSim. Why not just use Habitat 1.0 or Habitat 2.0 to perform these sim2real PointNav experiments? Perhaps there should be a baseline that compares training on different simulators to the real world performance. But, it seems like InteriorSim wouldn’t really have much of an advantage here, given the diversity and success of Habitat for PointNav.

**W4. Rendering speed is very slow.** Several minutes per frame for realtime ray tracing, 30-60 FPS for lower-quality renderings. This is significantly slower than most existing EAI simulators.

**W5. How were the objects created? How unique are they?** The paper mentions:
> Our artists modeled, textured, and semantically labeled 26,019 unique household objects from scratch using commercial and in-house geometric modeling tools. Our artists marked 17,234 of these objects as movable, and the remaining 8,785 as static.

However, the distribution of object types is very strange to me. Why are there over 1000 bookends, ornaments, and pillows? If the assets were manually created, why are there also over 1000 of them with an unknown asset type? Additionally, how diverse are these objects within the instances? To me, it would be hard to create 1000 unique pillows without a lot of overlap.

**W6. The segmentation results don't seem statistically significant.** Even at the highest rendering quality, it is barely beating out AI2-THOR. It seems like these numbers could be very noisy based on how the images were obtained from the simulators, and if there are exact 1-1 mappings from each simulator category to each NYU semantic segmentation dataset category.

Additionally, I don’t see any supplementary material that was mentioned in the paper, but maybe I am missing that.

**W7. Why only train on 50 InteriorSim environments?** The authors built up 300 scenes for InteriorSim, but only train on 50 of them. Why not just use all of them for the PointNav experiments? Are there problems with some of them?

**W8.** It would be nice to show more qualatitve examples of the scenes and objects. Currently, there are only a few pictures and it's hard to get a sense of what the scenes and objects actually are.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**N1.** As this is a simulator paper, with many very similar existing simulators previously built, it seems necessary for this paper to have some novel result that couldn’t be done before or a novel use-case for the field. Otherwise, I don’t see a good reason to accept or use this simulator as other ones have been built up for many years at this point and tested with many tasks.

**N2.** Mentioned above, but will relay here:
> **W3.** Sim2Real PointNav has been done many times before ([1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.06321), [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.05873), [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.10821)). Sim2Real PointNav isn’t a new capability unlocked by InteriorSim. Why not just use Habitat 1.0 or Habitat 2.0 to perform these sim2real PointNav experiments? Perhaps there should be a baseline that compares training on different simulators to the real world performance. But, it seems like InteriorSim wouldn’t really have much of an advantage here, given the diversity and success of Habitat for PointNav.

**N3. First novelty claim.** The first limitation of previous simulators mentions:
> Simulators that use artistcreated environments typically provide a limited selection of scenes (e.g., a few dozen homes, or a few hundred isolated rooms), which can lead to severe over-fitting and poor sim-to-real transfer performance. To work around this limitation, simulators often provide remixed variants of each scene (e.g., where objects have been arranged in different configurations), but this approach is limited by the diversity of scenes prior to remixing. On the other hand, simulators that use scanned 3D environments provide larger collections of scenes, but offer little or no interactivity with objects, and are therefore not suitable for tasks that involve rearranging the environment to achieve a particular goal (e.g., loading a dishwasher) (Batra et al., 2020).

Doesn’t ProcTHOR solve the issue with having massive amounts of interactive scenes?  300 scenes is small by those standards. It would be good to discuss it and add it to the table.

Additionally, for Table 1, why doesn’t iGibson 2.0, Habitat 2.0, and AI2-THOR have an infinite number of remixes? They all can shuffle objects, so it seems like there are a near infinite number of “remixes”.

**N4. Second novelty claim.** For the 2nd limitation of existing simulators, the authors mention:
> Simulators that use artist-created environments are often forced to provide simplified assets, because it is too labor-intensive to author high-resolution geometry and complex materials at scale.

This claim doesn’t seem true. AI2-THOR, iGibson 2.0, and Habitat 2.0 all have reasonably high quality assets that are manually constructed by professional 3D artists in some respect. Can you clarify what you mean by "forced to provide simplified assets"?
content.summary_of_the_review:
The authors do a lot of nice engineering work to build a simulator with an Unreal backend. However, the experiments are underwhelming and there aren't really any novel capabilities that this work enabled.

I would have liked to see more embodied experiments that justifiable why this simulator is better than the many other simulators. If the main advantage is photorealism, it would have been good to show that photorealism actually matters for sim2real. But for the sim2real experiment, the authors only render images at 160x90 and use lower quality settings, which defeats the point of having a highly photorealistic simulator.

Therefore, it doesn't seem like the paper is ready for publication.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: InteriorSim, with 300 carefully designed indoor environment, 2566 rooms and 17234 objects. InteriorSim is able to support path tracing for photorealistic rendering and RL training with Gym-style interface. The authors demonstrate the zero-shot transfer ability for the model trained in the simulation environment and deploy to the real world scenarios on several benchmarks like point-goal navigation and semantic segmentation task.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1. The paper is well-written and easy to follow. The presentation in the paper is fine

2. Lacking of high-quality assets is indeed a pain spot in embodied AI.

Weakness:

To me, the major contribution of this paper is a simulation platform and assets for house/room/object etc. It takes great efforts to make these features integrated into a system. 

1. The first concern to me is that: is a dataset/benchmark contribution in favor of ICLR community? I suspect it is more preferable in CVPR/ICCV/IROS/ICRA etc.

2. The benchmark tasks are not novel, point-goal navigation, semantic segmentation are quite standard tasks which have been supported by many previous simulation platforms. 
The semantic segmentation benchmark has compared the results with other simulation platforms but the point-goal navigation task does not. According to the results in semantic segmentation (table 4), I do not see a very significant improvements over the previous platforms like AI2THOR.

3. The key features of zero-shot transfer are mainly due to the powerful path-tracing rendering techniques provided by Unreal engines. Besides, path-tracing cannot be performed in real-time, which is also pointed out by the authors. In the real-time mode, the image quality (especially the illumination in the scene) should be largely affected. The author should take a more thorough analysis here. As all the benchmarks are based on the real-time mode.

4. More analysis for scenes and objects. Though the paper has a histogram for the distribution of the assets (Fig 3), I think it is quite basic. A more in-depth analysis is desired. For example:
a)	When the artists design the interior scene, do they have preference on design styles? How many artists are involved? Will the indoor styles be biased? Will the model trained in such scenes be biased? The author discussed the style limitation in supplementary materials. But I think it is an interesting problem to discuss openly. Because, we already have some assets for embodied AI. But how to make them more suitable for transfer with less efforts is more interesting.
b)	Are all objects are recreated? What’s the problem of existing CAD data repository like ShapeNet and PartNet-mobility? Do the object category choice have a deeper logic than ``they are common’’.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper writes well, and if the dataset is released I do believe many people in embodied AI will be interested.
But I do not think it is that original.
For the reproducibility. This work mainly proposes an unreal engine-based simulation platform and an asset repository along with it. I think they are reproducible, only takes a lot of engineering efforts and budget.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Given the contribution of this work is mainly on a platform and dataset, and the author failed to make a clear comparison to point out the advantages of their platform over previous platform, their dataset over previous dataset. Only simple statistical and baseline method comparison is not enough, which I also think is not extensive enough. We need more insights on the platforms and datasets.
Thus, I think this work need polishment before going to publication.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a photorealistic interactive simulator/environment for embodied AI applications and demonstrates that training a point-goal navigation policy in simulation can be zero-shot transferred to the real world.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
- The most photo-realistic interactive environment so far with Gym interface.
- Diverse scenes and assets with semantic labels which will be released open-source.
- A successful demonstration of zero-shot sim2real transfer for navigation.

Cons:
- It fails to show how photorealism is helpful for embodied AI tasks, as the main claim of the paper. I would expect a direct comparison between navigation policies trained on a non-photorealistic simulator vs InteriorSim and see how extra photorealism improves the performance (e.g. include results from training in other simulators in Table 2). There is only a marginal improvement over existing simulators on pre-training semantic segmentation (sec 4.3), though I appreciate that experiment.
- The demonstration of embodied AI applications is limited: only navigation task is implemented, and physics is limited to rigid-body only. 

Extra comments:
- Can you show the standard deviation in Table 2 since there is some randomness in data selection/training?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- This work is novel in terms of a photorealistic interactive learning environment.
- The paper is clear and well written, though the title is a bit overclaiming. In my opinion, a more appropriate title given the current state of the paper is “InteriorSim: A photorealistic simulator for indoor visual navigation”.
- I would expect more text on limitations compared to related existing embodied AI simulators.
content.summary_of_the_review: I highly appreciate the great effort in creating diverse assets, and I believe photorealism is important. Nonetheless, I would like to see more connections and benefits of InteriorSim to embodied AI tasks. Given the current state of the paper, it is not clear how researchers should use InteriorSim rather than existing simulators - if the extra photorealism outweighs the limited task and physics support.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work introduces a new photorealistic simulator for Embodied AI. The core features of the simulator are: (i) a new large set of scenes designed by artists and composed of many interactive objects, (ii) photorealistic rendering of environments and materials, (iii) a straightforward compatibility with OpenAI Gym. The differences between this and existing simulators are more content diversity, better physical interactivity and visual fidelity.

The paper presents quantitative (number of available scenes, objects, physical realism, photorealism) as well as qualitative comparisons between the introduced simulator and many state-of-the-art solutions. Another important part of this work is about showcasing the interest of such a photorealistic simulator to allow smooth sim-to-real transfer. Transfer of models trained on PointGoal Navigation and semantic segmentation is studied.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The proposed set of scenes and objects is very diverse and high-quality.
2. The high-quality path-tracing rendering mode option is novel compared to all previous Embodied AI simulators, and is a great feature when considering generation of a dataset to do offline learning. More generally, the different rendering modes as well as lighting configurations make this simulator the most configurable in terms of visual rendering.
3. Providing the ability to realistically interact with many objects is an important feature.
4. Experiments are detailed and thorough, and include real world studies, which is the end goal of Embodied AI.
5. The paper is well written and easy to follow.


Weaknesses:
1. I am a bit confused with how authors present the scenes, assets, objects as a feature from the simulator. Indeed, I would tend to disentangle a simulator from the assets it can load. The designed scenes are a great contribution for the community, but in my opinion can not be considered as a feature from the simulator. For example, in Table 3 in the paper, InteriorSim is compared to both datasets of scenes (Matterport3D, Replica, HM3D) and simulators (ThreeDWorld, AI2-THOR), or in Table 1 one can find information about number of scenes in Habitat 2.0. However, Habitat 2.0 is not a set of scenes, but a simulator that can load 3D assets. An interesting question is whether existing simulators (AI2-THOR, Habitat) could load the scenes introduced in this work.
2. Between 30 and 60 FPS as rendering speed is quite low when considering RL training applications that are a core part of the Embodied AI field. Training speed would indeed decrease again compared with what is presented in the paper (the numbers in the paper are properly introduced and seem fair) when adding training code, neural network inference.
3. Only two tasks are initially proposed with the simulator, and PointGoal Navigation was already introduced before and is currently solved in simulation (Wijmans et al., DD-PPO: Learning Near-Perfect PointGoal Navigators from 2.5 Billion Frames). It could be interesting to have more available tasks, but this is not a major concern as users of the simulator can define their own tasks.
4. There is no comparison with other simulators for the PointGoal Navigation Sim2Real transfer. There has already been work on Sim2Real transfer with other simulators, and it would thus be interesting to compare.
5. A few times in the paper, “in-house” processes are mentioned without details about the methods/pipelines. It would be great to have all methods described to ensure reproducibility of the work.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The contributions in this work are clearly stated, with supporting experimental studies comparing diverse baselines. The contribution shares many features with previous work, the most differentiating one being rendering options and quality. However, even if not very original, such strong engineering effort is key to the community and should be considered as an important contribution.
content.summary_of_the_review: Efforts in improving simulators used in Embodied AI are important to allow smoother transfer to the real world. This work, although not presenting a lot of novelties, is a strong step towards more photorealistic simulators. Various experiments regarding Sim2Real transfer support the claims in this paper. I am however concerned with a lot of the benefits in this work coming from the new designed scenes, assets, objects which are a great contribution but should be disentangled from the innovations on the simulation side. Moreover, better photorealism seems to come at the cost of a higher latency, which can be an issue when considering Reinforcement Learning training. All in all, I still feel like this work is promising, and am waiting for answers to my remarks from authors.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
